audience.programmeDescription: VU Literature and Society studies how literary texts shape and respond to culture and society. The English track combines close reading and theory with English literary history, language, creative writing and publishing, followed by a specialisation and individual thesis. A separate Dutch track concentrates on creative writing and Dutch literature.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Both UCR options include six literature courses. One emphasizes literary interpretation and visual culture. The other adds practice in life writing, poetry, public speaking and documentary. VU provides more specialist English literary history, language and publishing study, and requires an individual thesis.

curriculum.routeLabel: Literature and Society: English; Literature in a Changing World
curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC plan includes one 3 EC language option, a 12 EC specialisation sequence, a 12 EC individual thesis including its colloquium, and 30 EC of approved open study. Spring thesis entry requires passing all first- and second-year courses.

componentNotes.y2-pronpres: One 3 EC option applies. Native English speakers take Presentation and other students take Pronunciation.
componentNotes.y3-changingworld2: Entry requires participation in Literature in a Changing World 1.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: The 12 EC includes the colloquium. For spring entry, students must pass all first- and second-year courses.
componentNotes.y3-freechoice: Students can choose a minor, approved electives, study abroad, or an internship with electives.

ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

MCCLITR111.text: Introduction to Literary Studies introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation. Students examine what literature is, why it is read and studied, formal properties and the constructed character of texts. Fiction, poetry and drama are supplemented by contemporary nonfiction and basic film narration, developing critical terms, tools and techniques.

Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support literary analysis. A research paper, graphic explanation and creative retelling connect interpretation with narrative practice.

MCCLITR212.text: Life & Travel Writing examines memoir, autobiography, diaries, personal essays, travel writing and digital self-presentation. Students explore memory, identity, autobiographical truth, ethics and cultural positioning through close reading and theory. A personal writing portfolio and an independent life-narrative project connect analysis with practice.

Film history connects early cinema and major movements with feminist and postcolonial interpretation, alongside television, digital platforms and spectatorship. An analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory and scholarly research.

MCCMEDI211.text: From T.V. to TikTok examines American social history and everyday life from the mid-twentieth century through contemporary media. Television, film and digital forms connect storytelling and power with identity and imagined futures. Students compare dominant portrayals with Indigenous self-representation, investigate disability representation, and develop futures-oriented creative projects.

MCCMEDI212.text: Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.

Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.

Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.

Students connect grammar, discourse and cognition with interpretation through frameworks for dialogue, narration, modality, deixis and text worlds. Analysis exercises lead to an original research-supported stylistic analysis.

Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change. Close examination of paintings develops visual analysis, while a term paper combines study of a painting on location with art-historical evidence.

MCCHEAM212.text: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

MCCHEAM316.text: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
